objectives: State the protocol differences between UART, SPI, I2C.
Configure a peripheral via memory-mapped registers.
Distinguish polling, interrupt-driven, and DMA I/O.

slides.title: UART, SPI, I2C — the basic serial protocols
slides.body:
**UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter)**:
- 2 wires: TX, RX (no clock — both ends agree on baud rate).
- Frame: 1 start bit + 8 data bits + optional parity + 1-2 stop bits.
- Common baud rates: 9600, 115200, 1M. (Bps roughly = baud / 10.)
- Use: debug consoles, GPS modules, modems, Arduino-to-PC.
- Pros: simple, ubiquitous. Cons: short range; needs both ends to agree on baud.

**SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface)**:
- 4 wires: SCK (clock from master), MOSI (master out, slave in), MISO (master in, slave out), CS (chip select).
- Synchronous: master drives the clock; data shifts on each clock edge.
- Speed: up to ~50 MHz on modern MCUs.
- Use: SD cards, displays, sensors, FRAM, external ADCs.
- Pros: fast, full duplex, simple. Cons: many wires for many devices (1 CS per slave).

**I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit)**:
- 2 wires: SDA (data), SCL (clock). Both open-drain with pull-ups.
- Multi-master multi-slave: addressing by 7-bit (or 10-bit) slave address.
- Speed: 100 kHz (standard), 400 kHz (fast), 1 MHz (fast+), 3.4 MHz (high speed). 5 MHz with I3C.
- Use: sensors (temp, accel, gyro), EEPROMs, RTCs, port expanders.
- Pros: 2 wires for many devices. Cons: slower, more complex protocol (ACK/NACK, repeated starts), can lock up if a slave fails.

**The choice**:
- Need fastest? SPI.
- Need fewest wires + multiple slaves? I2C.
- Long cable to PC / debug console? UART.
- High-speed + long-distance? RS-485 (industrial), CAN (automotive), Ethernet.

slides.title: Memory-mapped peripherals + register interfaces
slides.body:
Peripherals on an MCU live in the **peripheral address region** (0x4000_0000+). Each peripheral exposes a set of **registers** at known addresses. Configuration + control = writing to these addresses.

**Example**: STM32F4 GPIO Port A. The base address is 0x4002_0000. Registers within:
```
GPIOA_MODER:   0x4002_0000 — mode (input/output/AF/analog) per pin
GPIOA_OTYPER:  0x4002_0004 — output type (push-pull/open-drain)
GPIOA_OSPEEDR: 0x4002_0008 — speed (low/medium/high/very-high)
GPIOA_PUPDR:   0x4002_000C — pull-up/pull-down
GPIOA_IDR:     0x4002_0010 — input data (read pin state)
GPIOA_ODR:     0x4002_0014 — output data (set pin state)
GPIOA_BSRR:    0x4002_0018 — bit set/reset (atomic set/clear)
...
```

In C: declare a struct mirroring the layout + cast the base address:
```c
typedef struct {
  volatile uint32_t MODER;
  volatile uint32_t OTYPER;
  // ...
} GPIO_TypeDef;
#define GPIOA ((GPIO_TypeDef*)0x40020000)

// Use:
GPIOA->MODER |= (1 << 10);  // pin 5 as output (MODER bits 10-11)
GPIOA->BSRR = (1 << 5);      // set pin 5 high (atomic)
```

**`volatile` is essential**: tells the compiler 'this memory may change without my code touching it'. Without `volatile`, the compiler might cache the read in a register + miss updates from hardware.

**Bit-set/reset register (BSRR)**: writing 1 to bit N sets pin N; writing 1 to bit (N+16) resets pin N. ATOMIC — no read-modify-write race. Critical for ISR-safe code.

**Vendor SDK / HAL**: instead of raw register pokes, vendor libraries provide `HAL_GPIO_WritePin(GPIOA, GPIO_PIN_5, GPIO_PIN_SET)`. More portable across MCU variants but bloats code + adds layers. Many production codebases use a hybrid: HAL for setup, raw registers in hot ISRs.

slides.title: Polling vs interrupt vs DMA
slides.body:
**Polling**: CPU repeatedly checks a status register until ready.
```c
while (!(USART1->SR & USART_SR_RXNE));  // wait for byte
char c = USART1->DR;                     // read it
```
Pros: simple, immediate. Cons: CPU 100% busy waiting. Useless if other work needs to happen.

**Interrupt-driven**: peripheral raises an interrupt when ready. ISR handles it. CPU is free meanwhile.
```c
void USART1_IRQHandler(void) {
  if (USART1->SR & USART_SR_RXNE) {
    char c = USART1->DR;
    enqueue(c);  // buffer for main loop
  }
}
```
Pros: CPU usable during waits. Cons: ISR overhead (~50 cycles entry+exit on Cortex-M); high-frequency events cause CPU thrashing.

**DMA (Direct Memory Access)**: hardware peripheral does memory transfers WITHOUT CPU. Configure source, destination, length; start DMA; CPU runs other code; DMA fires interrupt on completion.
```c
// Configure DMA stream to move from UART RX to a buffer
DMA1_Stream5->PAR = (uint32_t)&USART1->DR;  // source: UART data reg
DMA1_Stream5->M0AR = (uint32_t)rx_buffer;    // dest: RAM buffer
DMA1_Stream5->NDTR = 256;                    // 256 bytes
DMA1_Stream5->CR |= DMA_SxCR_EN;             // enable
// CPU now free to do other work while DMA fills the buffer
```
Pros: CPU completely free during transfer; high-throughput streams (SD card, ADC at MHz rates, audio). Cons: more setup; coherency considerations (DMA buffer must be in DMA-accessible SRAM, not cache-coherent without barriers on higher-end MCUs).

**The rule**: polling for one-shot ops; interrupts for moderate events; DMA for streams + high-throughput.

**Real example**: a UART receiving GPS data at 10 Hz × 100 bytes = 1 KB/s. Polling wastes CPU. Interrupts work but fire 1000×/sec — 50K cycles of overhead. DMA transfers each NMEA sentence + fires one interrupt per sentence — minimal CPU overhead.

question.question: Initialize an STM32 GPIO output pin
question.goal: Configure STM32F4 PA5 (LED on the Nucleo board) as a push-pull output, low speed, no pull-up.

steps.prompt: First, enable the clock to GPIOA. The RCC->AHB1ENR register has clock-enable bits; bit 0 = GPIOA. Code?
hints: You always need to enable the clock.
steps.reveal: `RCC->AHB1ENR |= RCC_AHB1ENR_GPIOAEN;` (or `(1 << 0)`). Without this, writes to GPIOA registers have no effect — a common gotcha for beginners.

steps.prompt: GPIOA->MODER is 2 bits per pin. For pin 5, bits 10-11. Mode 01 = output. Code?
hints: 2 bits per pin; pin 5 at bits 10-11; value 01.
steps.reveal: `GPIOA->MODER &= ~(0b11 << 10); GPIOA->MODER |= (0b01 << 10);` — first clear, then set, to avoid clobbering other pins' bits.

steps.prompt: OTYPER is 1 bit per pin; 0 = push-pull (default). PUPDR is 2 bits; 00 = no pull (default). So those don't need explicit setting. Now turn pin 5 high. Code?

options: `GPIOA->ODR |= (1 << 5);` — read-modify-write (works but not atomic, can race with ISR).
Both work; BSRR is preferred in ISR-safe code.

hints: BSRR is atomic + ISR-safe; ODR-RMW is not.
steps.reveal: `GPIOA->BSRR = (1 << 5);` is preferred. ODR-RMW works but has a race window if an ISR also modifies ODR.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Peripheral setup: enable clock → configure mode → use}}$$ The pattern is universal: clock-enable, mode-config, then use. Forgetting the clock-enable is the #1 STM32-newbie bug. BSRR vs ODR is the #1 race-condition source. Once you've internalized this pattern, you can read any vendor datasheet's GPIO chapter + write a driver in minutes.

question.question: Your audio application captures 96 kHz stereo 24-bit audio from an external ADC over SPI + writes it to an SD card over SDIO. What I/O strategy is appropriate?
options: DMA for both — SPI-RX DMA fills a buffer; when half-full, start SDIO-write DMA on the first half while SPI continues filling the second (double-buffering).
question.explanation: 96k × 2 channels × 3 bytes = 576 KB/s sustained throughput. Polling = 100% CPU. Interrupts = ~50k interrupts/sec from SPI alone (assuming 16-bit FIFO depth) — overhead destroys throughput. DMA with double-buffering: SPI-DMA fills one half while SDIO-DMA writes the other. Mid-buffer interrupt fires to swap. CPU has slack for other work. This is THE canonical embedded streaming pattern (audio, video, sensor capture).

slides.workedSolution: 576 KB/s is too fast for interrupts at the byte level. DMA does the transfer in HARDWARE. The mid-buffer interrupt at ~1 kHz (when half-buffer fills) is manageable. Pattern: dual buffers, swap on each half. SPI-DMA + SDIO-DMA run independently; CPU just coordinates the swap. Used in audio codecs, camera capture, EthernetMAC, etc.

question.question: UART at 115200 baud, 8N1 framing (8 data + 1 start + 1 stop, no parity). Approximate byte throughput?
I2C bus lockup
question.prompt: A team uses I2C for many sensors. Occasionally the bus 'locks up' — SCL stays low. Walk through the cause + the standard 'bit-bang the recovery sequence' fix.
Explain in two or three sentences why `volatile` is essential when accessing memory-mapped peripheral registers.
question.rubric: Mentions that the compiler optimizes away repeated reads of the same memory address (since it 'can't change'); for peripheral registers (which DO change asynchronously from hardware), this caching is wrong; `volatile` tells the compiler to always read/write the actual memory each time. Without volatile: missed updates, infinite loops on status bits, drivers that work by accident.
